query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A combined approach integrating rapid solidification processing (e.g., via selective laser melting or laser powder bed fusion) with high-speed in situ calorimetric and X‐ray diffraction characterization, and calibrated by CALPHAD modeling, can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume changes at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for high-entropy alloys over a wide compositional space.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys produced via conventional melting methods that may exhibit coarse microstructures and compositional segregation.
generation.intervention: Process HEAs using rapid solidification techniques (SLM/LPBF) to achieve fine-grained, more homogeneous microstructures followed by high-speed DSC and in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction during laser melting, with simultaneous CALPHAD predictions for calibration.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed under inert atmosphere with controlled high heating/cooling rates to minimize segregation during melting, ensuring uniform energy input.
generation.structural_mediator: Rapid solidification leading to refined grain sizes and reduced elemental segregation, which help in reducing measurement uncertainty of transition phenomena.
generation.mechanism: Rapid processing minimizes compositional gradients, and in situ measurements capture phase transitions with high temporal resolution. By correlating calorimetric signals and diffraction data with CALPHAD simulations, thermodynamic properties (melting temperature, enthalpy, entropy, and volume change) can be deduced accurately.
generation.predicted_outcome: The advanced method is expected to yield fusion temperature values within ±5–10% of CALPHAD predictions, alongside consistent values of enthalpy and entropy changes that are reproducible across different HEA compositions.
generation.baseline: Traditional DSC measurements on as-cast or conventionally melted HEAs, which suffer from coarse microstructures and compositional inhomogeneity that limit the accuracy of melting property estimation.
generation.boundary: This approach may be limited for HEAs with extreme compositional complexity or where ultra-high heating rates induce additional non-equilibrium phases that alter the melting transitions, and calibration uncertainties may arise in such cases.
generation.uncertainty: There is moderate uncertainty regarding the quantitative agreement between in situ measurement data and CALPHAD predictions across the entire HEA family, due to potential calibration and detection limits at high heating rates.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HEA samples using both conventional melting and rapid solidification techniques. Perform high-speed DSC and in situ X-ray diffraction during laser-induced melting while running parallel CALPHAD simulations. Compare the measured melting temperatures, enthalpies, entropies, and volume changes with the CALPHAD predictions.
measurements: Melting temperature via both calorimetry and diffraction-based phase transition detection
Fusion enthalpy and entropy determined from DSC peak integration
Volume change at melting from high-resolution in situ diffraction data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the determined thermodynamic properties (melting T, ∆H, ∆S, and ∆V) deviate by more than 10% from independently verified CALPHAD predictions consistently across multiple HEA compositions, or if the measurements cannot be reproduced across rapid solidification samples relative to conventionally processed ones, the proposed integrated method would be falsified.

Question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?. System: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at.% W, 20 at.% Ta, 20 at.% Mo, 20 at.% Nb, 20 at.% V). Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system (400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere); mixed elemental powders (20–70 µm) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; advanced trials parameters: 244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 0.10 mm hatch spacing, 0.03 mm layer thickness, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density, 67° layer rotation.. Test conditions: Density and Vickers hardness (HV10) measured; compression strength tested at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; electrochemical behavior assessed via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (scanning rate 0.5 mV/s)..
